retrieved: 2026-09-18 (B19-B22 added for targeted paid media and the dropship fulfilment structure)
scope: Margin, growth, unit-economics and audience benchmarks gathered specifically to support the Reserve Clinic margin-and-growth proposal. Every entry is third-party unless labelled analyst assumption. Figures were taken from search-result summaries; where a figure is load-bearing for the model it was corroborated across two independent queries. Treat all ranges as ranges, not point measurements.

benchmarks.topic: Public telehealth gross margin (closest listed comparable)
benchmarks.finding: Hims & Hers gross margin 74% FY2025 vs 79% FY2024; 65% in Q1 2026 and 63.8% in Q2 2026. Decline attributed to weight-loss offerings with shorter shipping cadences and higher fulfilment costs, plus international mix.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Ceiling reference for a telehealth blended gross margin. Reserve Clinic's Rx line is modelled well below this because it carries cold-chain shipping on every fill.

benchmarks.finding: Hims & Hers marketing expense was ~40% of revenue in Q2 2025 (down from ~46% a year earlier) and ~34.8% of revenue in Q2 2026 ($262.2M on $753.2M).
benchmarks.use_in_model: Anchors the paid-media-as-percent-of-revenue driver (25-32% by scenario). A celebrity-led brand should sit below this, not above, or the audience is not doing any work.

benchmarks.topic: DTC supplement gross margin and landed COGS
benchmarks.finding: Landed COGS (materials, packaging, manufacturing, inbound freight, duties) typically 20-30% of retail for a DTC supplement, producing 70-80% gross margin. Target range cited as 60-80%. Public DTC median gross margin ~57% for non-food categories. Per-unit COGS $3-15 depending on dosage form and volume.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Non-Rx line COGS driver set at 22-30% of retail.

benchmarks.finding: CAC $45-80 for supplements per triangulated industry estimates; $53-91 across ecommerce categories generally.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Sanity band for the computed blended CAC output. The model derives CAC rather than assuming it.

benchmarks.finding: 4-7% monthly when well run; 8-12% at health-and-wellness category average; 12-20% of subscribers churn in month 1 alone. Below 5% strong, below 4% top-tier, sustained above 10% a retention emergency.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Non-Rx subscription churn driver 5.5-9% monthly by scenario.

benchmarks.finding: AOV $30-65 monthly with 12-month LTV $300-600 (Recharge benchmarks cited). At 8% monthly churn a $40 subscriber at 55% margin returns ~$275 LTV. Healthy LTV:CAC 3.5:1 to 6:1, with 3:1 the floor.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Non-Rx AOV driver $68-88 (premium positioning above the cited band) and the 3.0x LTV:CAC gate.

benchmarks.finding: Sermorelin $96-199/mo via telehealth, $200-400/mo in-clinic. BPC-157 or TB-500 tissue protocols $100-300/mo. CJC-1295/ipamorelin stack $80-180/mo. Sermorelin plus CJC-1295 combination protocols $350-600/mo.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Rx programme price driver $199-299 per member-month, blended across protocols.
benchmarks.confidence: Medium (marketing pages and category guides, not a price survey)

benchmarks.finding: Asynchronous e-visits price at roughly $15-40 to the patient; raw median prices $20 (5-10 min) to $60 (21+ min). From the operator side a cited COGS breakdown is provider time $30, platform $10, support $10 per ongoing-care programme. Synchronous video $50-100.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Clinician cost per completed consult driver $32-45, and consult fee charged $49-79.

benchmarks.finding: Quoted base pack rate $1.95 per order plus $350/month cold storage for refrigerated peptide inventory; FedEx 2-Day temperature-controlled is the standard lane. Additional cost for insulated mailers, gel packs, refrigerated carrier surcharges. Most peptides require 2-8 C.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Cold-chain shipping driver $15-22 per Rx fill, which is the pack rate plus the expedited insulated lane, not the pack rate alone.

benchmarks.finding: 2025-2026 schedule cited as $975 application plus $2,150 annual per website; ~$3,125 year one for a single-site brand, ~$2,150/yr ongoing; expedited review ~$2,500 extra. It gates healthcare advertising on Google, Meta, Microsoft, TikTok, LinkedIn and Nextdoor, and is close to a prerequisite for card-not-present acceptance.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Certification line in opex. Also a gating dependency for the paid-media plan: no certification, no paid healthcare advertising at scale.
benchmarks.confidence: Medium (third-party summaries of a schedule that changes; confirm live)

benchmarks.topic: Market rate for turnkey white-label telehealth infrastructure
benchmarks.finding: One vendor's published pricing is $3,000-6,000 per month by plan tier plus a $5,000-10,000 one-time onboarding fee and separate per-consult fees, as of mid-2026. Other vendors advertise a flat monthly fee with zero revenue share including LegitScript and multi-pharmacy access; most gate pricing behind a demo. The category supplies licensed providers, HIPAA intake and EMR, e-prescribing, pharmacy fulfilment and the MSO / friendly-PC legal structure while the brand owns the customer.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Directly relevant to the stated $600/month flat fee. The model treats $600 as a platform/SaaS fee only and carries per-consult, medication, shipping and processing costs separately, because a fee at one fifth of the low end of published market pricing is very unlikely to absorb per-unit variable costs.

benchmarks.finding: Global peptide therapeutics estimated ~$58B in 2026 (estimates range $54.6B to $164B depending on scope), reaching ~$83.6B by 2030 at a cited 11.2% CAGR; most firms project 5-8% CAGR, some 10.8% to 2036.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Context only. This market is pharmaceutical-dominated and is NOT the addressable market for a cash-pay DTC brand. Shown in the proposal as context and labelled as such.

benchmarks.finding: Dietary supplements projected from ~$228.2B in 2026; nutritional supplements to ~$635.6B by 2030 at a cited 7.2% CAGR; dietary supplements cited at 7.2-9.5% CAGR depending on firm.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Growth context for the non-Rx line, which is the line that can operate in all fifty states.

benchmarks.topic: Celebrity-founded supplement brand outcomes (existence proof for the upside case)
benchmarks.finding: IM8, co-founded by David Beckham (~88M Instagram followers), reported $100M in 11 months and ~$120M ARR within the first year; its founders stated they deliberately did not lean on the fame but on product efficacy. Gruns reached profitability 14 months in with nine-figure ARR and a reported $500M valuation. For contrast, SHREDZ did $90k in its first year (2012) and $5M in 2013.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Calibrates the aggressive scenario. It establishes the outcome is achievable but the spread between SHREDZ and IM8 is roughly three orders of magnitude, which is why the scenario band is wide.

benchmarks.topic: Instagram performance at the 10M-plus follower tier
benchmarks.finding: Accounts above 10M followers average ~1.77% engagement, the lowest of any tier; accounts above 5M average ~1.97%, down ~24% year over year. Reels engagement averages ~3.8% and runs 3-5x static posts. Multiple sources note smaller creators convert to sales better than mega accounts despite lower reach.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Constrains the audience-conversion drivers. Engagement is not reach and reach is not purchase; the model steps followers to impressions to sessions to orders with a separate, explicit rate at each step and a decay curve on attention.

benchmarks.finding: Scott Disick (@letthelordbewithyou) reported at 27,410,219 followers as of June 2026; other trackers report 27M to 28.3M. Counts vary by refresh time.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Model input set to 27,400,000 and held constant across all three scenarios, because it is a measured quantity rather than a scenario choice. Audience quality, US share and health-category receptivity are NOT known and are handled by the reach and click-through drivers.
benchmarks.confidence: Medium (third-party trackers; not an audited or first-party figure)

benchmarks.finding: For the non-diabetic weight-loss population, discontinuation approaches 65% within the first year and 84.4% by 24 months. A real-world telehealth obesity provider reported programme retention of 78%, 63% and 58% at 3, 6 and 9 months. Commentary describes a 2026 'retention cliff' as the category's central problem.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Rx churn driver 9.5-13% monthly. This is the single most damaging assumption if wrong, and it is flagged as such in the sensitivity analysis.
benchmarks.confidence: Medium-High (peer-reviewed real-world evidence plus trade commentary)

benchmarks.topic: 503A bulk substances list movement on peptides, 2026
benchmarks.finding: On 15 April 2026 FDA removed 12 peptides from Category 2 of the 503A bulk drug substances list. First-batch substances under review include BPC-157, KPV, MOTS-c, Emideltide (DSIP), Epitalon, Semax and TB-500. The Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee met 23-24 July 2026 on Emideltide, Semax and Epitalon related substances, and FDA announced a further meeting before the end of February 2027 covering GHK-Cu, Melanotan II, Cathelicidin (LL-37), Dihexa acetate and PEG-MGF. Gonadorelin acetate has been added to Category 1. One category guide states CJC-1295 and ipamorelin 'returned to Category 1 in 2026'.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Not a financial driver but the gate on which products the Rx line may legally carry. The formulary must be re-verified against the live FDA list before launch and re-verified on each PCAC action; the CJC-1295/ipamorelin claim in particular rests on a single secondary source and is NOT treated as established.
benchmarks.confidence: Medium for the FDA actions, Low for the CJC-1295/ipamorelin Category 1 claim

benchmarks.topic: Retargeting versus cold prospecting economics, and the incrementality problem
benchmarks.finding: Retargeting ROAS averages about 4.2x in 2026, roughly 71% above prospecting; benchmark ranges given as 3-5x for prospecting and 5-10x for retargeting, with cold Meta prospecting typically 1.5-3x and retargeting often clearing 5x. Cost per acquisition drops 40-70% on retargeting audiences versus cold, and retargeting campaigns are described as costing 60-70% less than prospecting. Returning customers show a 3-4x conversion multiplier. CRITICALLY, the same sources warn that retargeting looks efficient mainly because it harvests demand prospecting already created, that cutting prospecting starves it weeks later, and that up to 75% of retargeting conversions may be non-incremental, with holdout tests showing true incremental lift of only 25-30%.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Sets cost per session and the conversion multiplier for the retargeting tier, AND sets the incrementality haircut driver (25-40% by scenario) applied to that tier's conversions. The haircut is the reason the model does not simply assume a better CAC: at the baseline 30% incrementality, retargeting's incremental CAC comes out roughly level with cold prospecting despite a much cheaper nominal CPA. The same logic sets a 35-55% incrementality haircut on paid branded search, which otherwise double-counts the partner's organic traffic.
benchmarks.confidence: Medium for the nominal efficiency figures, Medium-High for the incrementality warning (holdout-test based)

benchmarks.topic: Paid social creative performance, and the absence of a celebrity-specific benchmark
benchmarks.finding: Facebook traffic campaigns average about 1.71% click-through across industries and lead campaigns about 2.59%; roughly 1% or better is a practical 2026 target for paid social. Instagram feed ads run 0.22-0.88% click-through and Stories ads 0.33-0.54%. On creative: video content is cited at 30-50% higher click-through, including faces in visuals is a recommended practice, and social proof is credited with 15-25% higher conversion. NO study focused specifically on celebrity or recognisable-face ad performance lift was retrievable.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Sets cost per session on the cold prospecting tier. Also bounds the partner-creative cost-per-session discount driver (0.72-0.88), which is labelled a LOW-confidence analyst assumption precisely because no celebrity-specific lift benchmark exists. The model's validation method for it is a creative A/B test with and without the partner in month one.
benchmarks.confidence: Medium for the general paid-social figures, None for celebrity-specific lift (no source found)

benchmarks.topic: Wholesale-priced dropship fulfilment versus owning manufacturing runs
benchmarks.finding: Private-label supplements are cited at 40-60% gross margins, with a typical all-in per-unit COGS of $5-15 at a 500-unit minimum order and around $4 at 5,000 units (ingredients $2-7, dose form $0.50-2, bottle and packaging $0.75-3). Dropshipping is cited at 30-50% gross margins, with branded stores at 25-45% against 10-20% for generic dropshipping; one source states the per-unit cost in dropshipping is 'astronomically high, leaving you with virtually zero margin to reinvest in customer acquisition.' Named trade-offs are lower margins, limited product control and potential shipping delays. US manufacturing carries 2-3x the COGS of overseas with lower minimums and faster shipping.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Replaces the owned-inventory cost structure with the arrangement the project owner described: wholesale unit pricing from a wholesaler who holds the stock and ships to the customer. The non-prescription cost-of-goods driver is now an ALL-IN wholesale cost including the wholesaler's pick, pack and ship, set at 32-44% of retail by scenario, and the separate per-order fulfilment driver is zeroed because it is bundled. Inventory months are set to zero, removing the working-capital draw entirely. The important arithmetic: owning runs at the benchmark 26% landed COGS plus $7.50 of separate fulfilment is about 36% of retail all-in on a $78 order, so wholesale dropship at the 37% baseline is close to MARGIN-NEUTRAL and hands back the cash. The cost is not margin today, it is the absent improvement curve: an owned run drops to roughly $4 per unit at 5,000 units, while a wholesale price does not fall that way, so bringing manufacturing in-house becomes a real and quantifiable margin lever once volume justifies it.
benchmarks.confidence: Medium. The per-unit manufacturing figures are reasonably consistent across sources; the cited dropship margin bands mix generic reselling with private-label and wholesale arrangements and should not be applied directly. A wholesale price schedule from the named wholesaler replaces this entire range.

benchmarks.topic: Own-label distributor liability: a dropship arrangement does not transfer FDA or FTC responsibility
benchmarks.finding: FDA states that an own-label distributor is 'ultimately responsible' for the quality of the dietary supplement products it places into interstate commerce. FDA has stated that a firm has 'ultimate responsibility to ensure that all phases of the production of those products are in compliance with cGMP requirements' and that 'although your firm may contract out certain manufacturing operations, it cannot contract out its ultimate responsibility to ensure that the dietary supplement is not adulterated for failure to comply with dietary supplement cGMP requirements.' A firm that packages, labels or distributes a supplement manufactured by another firm is subject to the dietary supplement cGMP rule for the operations it performs. Commentary notes that a supplier's claim to be 'GMP certified' does not shift liability, that FDA and FTC hold the brand owner responsible for label and marketing claims, and that supplier contracts frequently state the brand alone is accountable for label claims.
benchmarks.use_in_model: Not a financial driver. It is the reason the dropship structure does not reduce the brand's legal exposure, and the reason the legal and quality line items are NOT cut alongside the inventory line. It also raises the specific stakes here: the product carries a named public figure, so a quality or claims failure by a third-party manufacturer becomes that person's reputational problem and the brand's legal one.
benchmarks.confidence: High (FDA guidance and FDA compliance programme, corroborated by independent legal and laboratory commentary)

not_retrievable: First-party analytics for any competitor (sessions, conversion rate, CAC, churn) — no traffic tool or ad library was reachable.
Audited financials for any private peptide or celebrity supplement brand. IM8 and Gruns revenue figures are self-reported via press.
Scott Disick's audience composition (US share, age, gender, health-category affinity) and any historical conversion performance on a paid endorsement.
The identity, licences, contract terms, insurance, pharmacy network and LegitScript status of the $600/month provider — no provider was named.

Any study quantifying the advertising performance lift from celebrity or recognisable-face creative. The creative-discount driver is an analyst assumption supported only by general findings on video and faces in visuals.
A branded-search conversion-rate multiplier benchmark, and any benchmark for branded-search volume generated per unit of social reach. Both are analyst assumptions.

Whether the proposed partner's likeness rights extend to paid media. Organic posting rights and paid-usage rights are separately licensed, and health-category ad review plus LegitScript certification gate the paid use regardless.

The named dropship partner's unit price schedule, stock allocation, cGMP certification, third-party testing regime, certificates of analysis, shipping service levels and indemnity terms. No partner was named, so the cost of goods is a benchmark range rather than a quote.

Whether the dropship partner can absorb a celebrity-launch demand spike without a stockout. Capacity in the model is an analyst assumption; a committed stock allocation in writing is the only way to replace it.
